utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. I am Defence counsel Petar Puliselic, Defence counsel for Dragan Papic, the accused, and I would like to ask you several questions. You said that up until 1990, that is to say, that from 1990, you had been living in Vitez, and that you lived in Busovaca prior to that, as far as I understood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were born in Pirici and that you grew up there. Did you go to Pirici often and who did you stay with, if you went there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: While I lived and worked in Busovaca, I would usually go to visit my parents in Pirici every weekend. Usually I would stay with them. Sometimes I would go to our neighbours if there was a holiday of any kind or any kind of celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: How do you know Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dragan Papic belongs to the younger generation, he's younger than me, and we did not actually grow up together, this being the case, but when we were already grown up, we knew each other, and I'm a good friend with his father and, of course, we're neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can I take it then that you knew him well?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, relatively well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Dragan Papic worked?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dragan Papic is, by profession, a forestry expert, and he worked in the forestry department together with my father-in-law, my wife's father. My late father-in-law was called Andrija Musa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you see Dragan Papic in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you notice anything special on his face?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can see that he has a beard which is well-shaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know, at the end of 1992 or 1993, whether he had a beard at that time?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had a bigger beard than the one he has now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dragan Papic had any extreme nationalist positions with regard to the Muslims and did he discuss politics in an extremist fashion?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't have any knowledge as to that, and knowing his father, I don't believe he did because it is common knowledge that his father had very good relations with the Muslims of Ahmici, especially when the waterworks and water supply for the village was being constructed, and I can say that there were especially good relations on the part of the whole of the Papic family with the(redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Dragan Papic's hobbies were, what he did during his leisure time, out of working hours?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, together with his brother Goran, he used to repair cars in his spare time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did he repair cars for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he repaired everybody's cars in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You have already said something about his father, Ivo Papic. Do you know whether he does water supply installations for the Muslims today who have returned to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he is working on the construction of the waterworks network and supply network in Ahmici today, but I do know that he does work between Kremenik and Grbavica, he does maintenance work for the water supply system, and in the Grbavica village, the houses have been repaired, and it is common knowledge that they were all returned to the Muslims last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that he also saw to the water supply installations in the mosque, that he worked on that project?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether, in his free time, he was helped by Dragan in this work?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I did not see this myself, but usually, on construction work of this kind, it was usual for the children to help their parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that work on the mosque was done by Ivo Papic without any remuneration, that he did it free of charge?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that when the mosque was opened, there was a big inauguration ceremony, I think you said this yesterday, in Ahmici. Did many people attend from the surrounding parts? Did people come in by buses and private cars? Do you remember whether there were a lot of buses and cars?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that day very well. The entire area, from the Topolsko cemetery up to Papics' house, that is a cousin of Dragan Papic, and right up to my own family house, was turned into a parking lot, and the Muslims used this for prayer, prayer area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these buses were parked in the field owned by Papic?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that area too was set aside for a parking lot for buses because there were several thousand people in the area who, had they come by car and parked, would have taken up all the space around the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Hadzija Ahmic Hazim expressed his gratitude to the fact that the vehicles were allowed to park on his own land? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did express his thanks and gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us, in closing, what kind of man was Dragan Papic? Was he violent? Was he a peace-loving man? Was he ready to help others? What was his conduct towards the Muslims? Did he have Muslim friends? Was he friendly with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as being sociable and having friends, all of us living in that area were friends with our next-door neighbours. We would socialise. And very often we would go out together. As far as the character of Dragan Papic himself, I can say that he was, by nature -- he took after his father a great deal, and his father was a very hard worker, he was well-known for being a hard worker, and he liked to joke a lot. The same character traits were inherited by his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Was he violent? Did he enter into conflicts of any kind?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Puliselic. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, good morning to you, sir. My name is Michael Blaxill. I am one of the team of Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I do have a few questions for you, sir, arising out of the evidence you have given here this morning. You have just described the considerable ceremony when the mosque was opened, the large private mosque with the minaret. Do you feel that that was obviously appreciated as a significant building in the area by the local Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did that perhaps make Ahmici a rather significant and special place in the minds of Muslims within the Lasva Valley area?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not at that time, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you think, in its short life, the mosque actually became a significant and special place for the Muslims of that area?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that it was a significant place only for the Muslims from Donja Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can go back a little? You say that you did your military service or left the JNA in 1981; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the end of 1980. On the 12th of December, 1980, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Since that time, you have been professionally engaged in the telecommunications world; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. From the 15th of January, 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In terms of any ongoing obligations to serve the state in a time of peace or war, you have worked exclusively, your assignments were in telecommunications?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively in telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you have already indicated that there were essentially two networks, one for the military and one purely civilian, in terms of telephones, is that right, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I said that within the telecommunications system of the post office, there were no military connections, and what kind of network they had and what kind of system, that, I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you received your subsequent assignment, you know, for a situation perhaps of wartime, did that bring you into any involvement with the military communications, or did you remain exclusively involved in civilian communications?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: As the war broke out, I did not receive any orders to work on military communications, and as regards my war assignment, in terms of work duty, it was reduced entirely to the field of civilian telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. So if I can now turn to the post-election period of -- we will move towards 1992. You have confirmed that you were not active in politics yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But you supported the -- I believe you called it the Croatian Democratic Community; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, during 1992, is it correct that an institution was formed called the HVO in Central Bosnia and indeed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean, whether this institution was organised? Do you mean whether it was organised officially and whether I was part of this institution, or am I simply aware of the fact that it existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, your awareness of its existence. You were aware of it, sir, were you?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of its existence. There was a government, a municipal council. I think it was called the HVO government, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you endeavour to keep yourself aware of current affairs in the area as time passed, political developments and the like?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I read the newspapers and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So presumably, from that standpoint, you became aware of the aims of the Croatian Community in Herceg-Bosna, you became aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean "intention"? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you become aware of the creation, shall I say, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it true that some of the expressed aims of that community were a degree of Croatian autonomy, territorial, economic, and, to that extent, military self-determination?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: As 1992 progressed, did you become aware that the BiH government in Sarajevo actually declared the HVO government to be illegal? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. What I do know, though, is that in 1992 there was a referendum for Bosnia and Herzegovina and that we voted. But I am not aware of this proclamation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the later half, we will say, of 1992, in the municipality of Vitez, there was ostensibly a power-sharing between a Muslim governmental body and the HVO governmental body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the second half of 1992, and until the end of 1992, there was a joint government in the municipality of Vitez, to the best of my knowledge; that is to say, that there was an executive branch in the municipality. It was some kind of municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, as we approached October 1992, would it be fair to say that the effective governing power in the Vitez area had become the HVO municipal government; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until October, I think that the joint government was still operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But after October 1992, I presume from what you're saying, that was no longer the case?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, after October '93 -- I'm sorry, '92, to the best of my knowledge, the Muslim part of the leadership, the municipal leadership, established their own war presidency or whatever it was called, I do not know the exact name, and it was located in the Mahala, that is to say, in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You refer to it as a war presidency, but would it not be fair to say that, except for the incidents on the 20th of October, between Muslims and Croats, there had been no outbreak of conflict to that time?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were some registered incidents until October 1992. Rather, before October 1992, there weren't any incidents of this nature, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you say that your Muslim staff members from the post office stayed away from work for seven days after the 20th of October; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It was put to you that the law of that time would have normally meant their immediate dismissal for staying away so long; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was that a law from the BiH government or was that a law perhaps created by the HVO municipal government?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, it was a law that was enforced by the community of the Yugoslav PTT, and all of us working in the post office worked according to those regulations and those laws that were operative then within this unified PTT system of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When the Muslim employees returned to work, you obviously decided not to enforce that law. What made you take the more sympathetic course of action that you took?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I simply didn't want anybody to abuse that, and I didn't want it to be characterised as discrimination by anyone. I did not make this kind of decision on my own. I consulted the other employees as well. We thought that this was a fair thing to do to our colleagues, and if we had to defend what we did in terms of the law on PTT, we were prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At that time, those colleagues had expressed certain fears to you. Can you tell us what those fears were?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, they did not describe in detail what they were afraid of. They simply said that they were afraid. Although they were aware that there were no reasons for this, the explanation was, "We were afraid."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Vidovic, with respect, as an employer who would have the legal right to dismiss those people for an apparent breach that warranted dismissal, did you not see fit to inquire more as to what their fears were that justified their staying away?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I tried, but I did not hear about any details from any one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In any event, you decided not to dismiss these employees?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I forgot to mention a few minutes ago that when people were on duty at the post office for longer periods of time, which is what we discussed earlier on too, all of us practically had earned three times seven days off. We were entitled to days off. So I remember now, I distinctly remember now, that we treated those seven days as days off that had been earned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Now, do you not consider it was coincidental that the events of the 20th of October led to that sudden seven-day absence of your Muslim employees?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it did coincide with that day, but in my opinion, there was no need for that event that occurred by the cemetery to affect their coming or going from work, because at that point in time, the situation in the post office where we worked was perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I were to suggest to you, sir, that a logical conclusion may have been that they were frightened of the HVO, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what they were to be afraid of. That would be my answer. Had they called me, I would have been prepared to protect each and every one of them for sure with regard to any matter, and I really have no idea what they feared at that time in October and why they didn't come to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll move on from that subject now, sir. Mr. Vidovic, you made reference to Vitez at the time having a jointly-manned police station, both Muslim and Croat police officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, after the elections, a joint government was formed in the municipality and in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there a point at which that ceased to be a joint police station and consisted of only one ethnic group of police officers?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this happened along parallel lines. When the government was formed in Mahala, I don't know whether "war presidency" is the right word, but that resulted in the establishment of a separate police station in Mahala, in Stari Vitez, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: After the war, there remained a police station in Vitez, is that correct, a Croat-manned police station?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean "remained"? You mean the building itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The actual institution of a detachment of police.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At this time, are there any Muslim employees working at that police station, to your knowledge? You may not know, sir.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but what period are you exactly asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm saying even as of today, now, 1999?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Today, in 1999, in the police station in Vitez, there are Muslim policemen, as far as I know, in accordance with the census from 1991, which is to say, I think that the situation now is about half/half. I could not give you the exact proportions, but if the chief of police is a Croat, then his first commanding officer is a Muslim, and that is the way it goes down the hierarchy lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, if I can return to the beginning of 1993, at the post office in Vitez, you indicated that, as the conflict approached, the HVO government itself took up residence in that building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that at the beginning of the conflict, the leadership of the municipality came to reside in the post office, not the HVO government. I used an expression of my own, the leadership of the municipality. I'm saying the mayor, for example, the head of the government, and his immediate associates. On the 17th, I think it was. On the 16th, they didn't because I didn't go down into basement on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I probably misled you by a misquote on my part, Mr. Vidovic. I apologise. I believe you also said that the information office, the 985 number, was also located within the building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you have any personal contact with those elements, with the local leadership and with the information office?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I shall try to explain how it came to be that the reporting centre was housed in the basement of the post office. When the building was actually constructed in 1984, then a contract was signed between the municipal government at the time and the post office envisaging premises for the reporting centre in the basement, and they even had an entrance of their own. Later, it turned out that the reporting centre -- I'm sorry, turned out to be a lessee here because there was always the problem of joint expenses. I'm talking about the situation until 1993, that is. As regards contact with people from the reporting centre, I can say that it was only based on what we had in common, that is to say, when there were power shortages, then using joint facilities such as the toilets, et cetera. I know all the people who were in the reporting centre, of course, this centre on reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you have any day-to-day professional dealings with these people in the early part of 1993 when they moved in?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: We would see each other every day, but professionally, no, except for our communication on the telephone and their interventions to repair certain breakdowns for certain subscribers, when they would intervene on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But you say also you had personal contacts with them. Did these people, in any way, keep you abreast of events in the locality and what was developing?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean about everything, all events or, perhaps, certain excessive things?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I should suggest developments on a political level or incidents that may have occurred in various locations in the area, relations between ethnic groups, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, certain bits of information, yes, in passing, but nothing official, nothing in our official relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Again, you have already said that you did try to keep yourself abreast of current affairs and what was happening in your region; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I read the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just before I move on to the events of April of 1993, you mentioned an encounter between your sister and Mr. Berbic and some village guards in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it true, in fact, that after he told your sister not to be afraid, it was only a drill, there was no aggressive action by any of these village guards or Muslims in Ahmici right up to the 16th of April? There was no such incident, was there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those days, when I received that information, as far as I know, there wasn't any activity on their part. I'll try to remember. I think that this encounter between her and them was in November because she went to work -- yes, yes, November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon me. It would seem that there was no problem from that side subsequent to November '92 that gave any physical threat to the Croats in Ahmici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards my sister, no, no, nothing except for this encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, if I may move to the events of the 15th onwards of April 1993. You were at work on the 15th when you said you were organising fuel supplies. I believe that's so?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps I have misunderstood the shift. Did you work -- on that day, did you work during the day or was that when you did the shift from 8.00 p.m. to 7.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: All of us worked every day from 7.00 until 3.00, and the shifts rotated. On the previous night between the 14th and the 15th, I cannot recall who was on duty, but in an already established order, I was supposed to be on duty between the 15th and the 16th from 8.00 p.m. until 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you said you did perform that duty?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that night, I did perform that duty, and I was lucky. There were no power shortages, so I didn't have to intervene, but, yes, I was there on duty that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Presumably, you were able to gain some sleep during that night?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. All those doing shifts would usually spend the night sleeping, especially if there were no power cuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And that leads to the fact that you were awakened by the sound of gunfire the following morning?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was not awoken by the alarm or by any power cuts or anything else but by shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was it a normal procedure for you to check the automatic printout for defective telephone numbers when you started any period of work or was there a special reason to do so that morning?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did our shifts in the main building, and every morning, when we would come to work at 7 a.m., the computerised exchange would give out all sorts of alarms, both major alarms and medium importance alarms and other ones. And that morning, when I woke up, that is to say when I was woken up by the shooting, standard procedure was to wait for the alarm list printout which comes out at 7 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to ask the Prosecutor -- I would like to ask you to warn the Prosecutor not to ask questions that have already been answered. During the examination-in-chief, the witness expressly explained to the Trial Chamber that it was standard regular procedure in the post office that the list with the defective telephone numbers was put out at 7.00 a.m. every morning. So the questions posed by the Prosecutor are questions that have already been answered. I didn't want to interfere, but would you please ask him not to ask questions that have already been asked, but to pose them, perhaps, in a different manner if he wishes to pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I take Mr. Radovic's point. I was, however, laying foundation as to whether or not the events of the gunfire had influenced the witness's actions at that time in relation this particular thing. That was all. I am moving away from that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, you say that you asked the operator to perform a specific check for defective numbers; can you please tell us what motivated you to make that request?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that as the operative man, and the only person who was there and performing the role of operator, between 7.30 and 8.00 a.m., once again, requested of the computer to -- that is, regardless of the fact that it had printed out the 7.00 list, without any defective numbers, to check again and see whether any lines were defective. I supposed that the shooting that I had heard and the detonation that I had heard that some aerial lines had possibly been damaged. And as at 7.00 that morning, nobody turned up to work, as I was alone in the exchange, I felt that this kind of regular reading of the defective numbers would mean less work. Because it is common knowledge that a computerised telephone exchange, if there are many defective numbers, can go to a restart, which means that the telephone numbers which were all right would have been put out of action. And so between half past 7.00 and 8.00, I asked for a reread from the computer, to see whether there were any subscribers' numbers which were defective.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I noted in the course of the transcript one expression I would like to clarify with you, because the expression was used of "we cut off lines to Stari Vitez," and I'm just wondering, was that a positive action taken at your end, that you had to disconnect those lines? Or was it some other cause?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, quite obviously I was misunderstood, or that something was not well written down in the transcript. What I said was that through the Mahala, that is to say the old part of Vitez, there was a cable, a cable existed, which supplied all the subscribers in the Mahala and Stari Vitez, and all the subscribers in the villages of Donja Veceriska, Gornji Veceriska, Zaselje, Krcevine, Jardol, Kremenik, and others. When somebody would say that there was a defective line, and some people had already said that the telephones were not working in those villages, we used a special instrument that we had in our possession, and it is known in the telecommunications system. And by measurement and by using this device, we were able to ascertain that the whole cable was out of order, at some points, let's say 848 metres, at a point 848 metres away. From the plans and projects and those documents, and on the basis of our own measurements, we were able to ascertain the exact point and location. I said that this location was opposite to the house owned by Enes Sehic, because that was where a concrete grid or shaft existed. I also said that in 1994, when we put this part of the cable -- repaired this part of the cable, we were able to see how this cable had been cut. So we didn't cut it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Your Honours, I do note that the time is 12.10, and as we've just been speaking of lines being cut, I just wonder if you would wish to take your briefer break at this time. I am virtually about to -- well, almost to change subject matter. There's two more -- I can I think almost guarantee you we shall finish well in time this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we will take now the 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I may return, Mr. Vidovic, to the events in Vitez on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, once you discovered that a lot of phone lines, all the phone lines to Stari Vitez had gone down, and you ascertained had been cut. Were you aware of any activities of the HVO in Vitez at that time of day?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that the lines towards Stari Vitez two days later, not the 16th, two days after the 16th, two days after the 16th we ascertained that the lines were down. They were working on the 16th. If you're asking me about the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must have misunderstood you. I thought your indication was that -- please correct me if I'm wrong -- is that on the morning of the 16th, you asked the operator to do a check and discovered a large number of lines were inoperable.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was the operator. I asked the computer, I put in the request of the computer to list out all the lines that were down. The computer did so, complied, and the list did not contain the numbers which were in Stari Vitez and further away. They were in the town, and they were all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll return to the question of whether you were aware of the activities of any of the HVO military on the morning of the 16th in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything like that on the 16th and afterwards, as I was alone. I said that nobody turned up to work. And so I spent the entire time at the exchange. I don't know the activities, there was just shooting the whole morning, and the whole day, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From where you were working within the exchange, could you in fact see out of the building?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Let me explain why not. When the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and when the JNA started the shelling of towns, we in Vitez protected many of the buildings with regard to shelling and the shattering of glass. This kind of protection was also done on the post office building; that is, we had 12-centimetre-thick planks put up, and of course we couldn't see anything through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you hear later, from any sources, about the actions of the HVO in Vitez that day, including perhaps roundups of Muslims, detention of Muslims, holding of Muslims in the cinema, which you have mentioned. Did you hear of any of those activities occurring that day, told about them?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not on that day. I had no information on that day, apart from the fact that I mentioned a moment ago that there was a serious conflict in Ahmici, and there was shooting the whole day. I cannot define who was in charge of these activities, but shooting could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We'll return to the question of the detention of civilians. Did you become aware at some future time of the Kaonik camp, and that the number of Muslims in Vitez were transferred to there? Did that information reach you at some point?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Later on, let me say about a year later, I knew that a prison had been organised at Kaonik. But in those first few days, and I think that that's what you're interested in, I had no information in that respect, nor did I hear of people being transferred to Kaonik and who did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have stated that you were at work on the 16th in the exchanges, and that you were not at any time in Ahmici that day. That is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the next few days as well, not only on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I presume therefore during those days you did not see any of the accused you've mentioned: Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Mr. Papic or Mr. Josipovic? I presume you can not see any of those people over those days. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. For the first five days, I practically saw nobody, apart from the fact that on the third day, I went home, I had a small baby in Vitez, and I spent one hour there and returned. The reason was as I have said, was that I was alone in the telephone exchange, because in those first few days nobody came to work apart from me, because I found myself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Had you had any contact by telephone or otherwise with your family, your mother and your sister, just prior to the 16th of April? Had you spoken to them, say, on the 15th, or on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Very often. I said that they were alone, and so I contacted them frequently, both by telephone and also every five or six days I would go and visit them, because I had a baby, and my mother had a cow, and at that time, I would take milk. Apart from that contact, and for looking after them in that way, to see that everything was all right, it was also this formality that I would carry out, I would go and collect the milk and have the milk ready for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying to you, sir, that they did not express any particular fears or worries to you, did they, in those days just before the 16th?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: They did express anxiety, and they thought they had in mind everything that took place in places around Vitez. I said Gornji Vakuf, as a case in point. Novi Travnik, Busovaca. Their house is the first house next to the Muslim houses, and of course they were afraid. That fear of theirs in some way was appeased by our telephone conversations and the contacts that I had with them. At least to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So whilst they had the anxieties clearly before the 16th of April, they had not been in any way subjected to physical attack or the threat of physical attack from anywhere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were not subjected to threats or physical attacks apart from the fact that this fear existed, this anxiety existed, and I explained a moment ago why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You made reference to the events of Ahmici, when you found out about them, as being a "strong conflict," I think is the expression, with heavy losses on both sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is the information that I heard on that particular day expressed in that way, that there was a strong conflict or serious conflict and that casualties existed on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you made aware of the number of casualties -- I know you've answered about not knowing the number specifically -- but did anyone indicate to you proportions relating to civilians or to military people who may have perished and been wounded in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that first day, nobody knew. We heard a figure bandied about, some ten people, approximately. But later on, we heard that the figure involved was actually 50 to 60. So in the days that followed, we got this information from informal meetings with the people that I could have contacted from the telephone exchange. Of course, none of this was actually proved. At that time -- and the information I received, we were not able to conclude whether they were civilians or soldiers or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you made reference to one person you believe died that day, Mr. Mirjan Santic. Are you sure that that was the date of his death?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. On that day, I did not know who had been killed. Several days later, however, I learnt that amongst the casualties was Mirjan Santic. Not Sandic, Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Santic. Forgive my pronunciation, Mr. Vidovic. Sir, I would like just to have you look at one document, this is Prosecution Exhibit 337, please. The document has already obviously been in evidence, Your Honours. It is the HVO's list of members killed. Now, Mr. Vidovic, I would be grateful if you would firstly look at page number 14 and at number -- or at least it's 14 in the translation. Let us look to number 435 of the list of casualties. That might assist you better.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are only ten pages here, not 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There should be upwards of 18 but ... It does not go up to 435?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have, on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's, I think, the difference between the translations, Your Honours, and the original language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You see number 435. That is Mr. Mirjan Santic, son of Franjo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You will see there, sir, the date given was, in fact, the 18th of April but ... You knew him?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you knew him to be a soldier in the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was. What do you mean "soldier"? A professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, a member of the HVO and in the military at that time. Perhaps conscripted, perhaps not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know the details and his status.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you have a look at the very front page then, please, sir? Would you agree that that appears to be an HVO document listing HVO members who were killed?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: How do you mean, do I agree? Whether it is an authentic copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm just asking: Is that what the document appears to be to you? Others will authenticate.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a list of people killed. I think that a document would have a different form.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Does the list express itself to be a list of HVO people killed?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, perhaps. I don't know. I don't understand what you're asking me, actually. What do you mean by whether we can accept it as being a document of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What I'm asking, Mr. Vidovic, is simply this: On the face of that paper that you have in your hands, does that appear to be under the title of "A List of Members of the HVO who were Killed"? I'm not asking you to verify that as an official document or anything of that nature. Thank you. That's not what I'm asking. Is that what it appears to be?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, a list -- like a list, yes. It looks like a list. But whether all the people on the list are members of the HVO, I cannot tell you at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would ask you to move on to just one further task for me, if you would be so kind? In the column under the name "Place," if you would just very briefly cast your eye down that single column "Place" on each of the pages in your possession, and can you see whether the name "Ahmici" appears there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not Ahmici, no. But we have Santici, Pirici. Pirici, of course. Pirici. Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me, would you, the word "Ahmici" doesn't appear, but there are a few entries for Pirici and perhaps Santici with varying dates; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. No, there isn't any mention of Ahmici. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Oh, just one further thing. You stated that you know Mr. Marijan Santic. Do you recall what his profession was and how you knew him? Was he a co-worker or friend?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we were not very close, but I know him from the time when he dated his now wife, and at that time, while they were still dating and when I was dating my present-day wife, we used to go out together for drinks or something like that, and I know him from those days and I know his wife very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic. I thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Let us start just as the Prosecutor cross-examined you. The new mosque built by Hazim, what was its significance for the villagers of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was important for the villagers of Donji Ahmici because they did not want to participate in the building of the upper mosque, and the lower mosque was built without any financial participation of their own, it was built for them, and they actually got a place of worship in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: So that was one thing. And it was also important for them because of its position and because they gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when the Muslims would build a mosque, how were financial resources -- I mean, how was this financed? Was it financed through voluntary contributions or in other ways? That's what my question really is.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I could not give you a very precise answer, but I'll tell you what I do know. I think that in that part too, they would allocate a certain amount per family, per household, and these records were kept either by hodza or by the village mufti. That is one way of building it. The other way is by donations from Islamic countries, through the Islamic religious community, so that is another way which exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in addition to the hodza or the imam, was there an organisational form of citizens who exercised control over what was happening within the mosque and around the mosque and related to religion? Specifically, do you know about the committee of the Islamic religious community?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain what that is. If you know, of course, if you know. I know that you are not Muslim by religion, so tell me what you know about the committee of the Islamic religious community, only what you know.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, what I know is the following: In every municipality, there was a committee of the Islamic religious community which, in every village, organised a subcommittee or whatever we would choose to call it. Well, never mind. Call it what you will. And this subcommittee or committee was headed by the hodza or any of the clergymen, and subcommittees were headed by the mufti. That's what we called him. This is not a religious teacher, but it is a man in a village whose task is to communicate with people. And if a mosque is being built or if any kind of activity is being carried out, he is in charge of it as some kind of a committee or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. To the best of your knowledge, as regards the new mosque, the lower mosque, the one belonging to Hazim, the hodza, which citizens of Ahmici went there to pray and which citizens went to the mosque in Upper Ahmici to pray, if you can answer this, of course?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, I'm going to tell you what I know. In Gornja Ahmici, Hazim's brother lived there and still lives there until the present day, and he is the only one with his family who prayed in the lower mosque, in Hazim's mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So Hazim's mosque is the lower mosque; right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. And Abdulah Mustafa, I cannot remember anymore, Sakib, Nezir, et cetera, these neighbours who live near the lower mosque also went there. They would go to pray from Donja Ahmici, but I think that nobody but the brother prayed in the lower mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about the significance of the lower mosque for the other Muslims. Please tell me, did you see Muslims from other villages coming to pray in the lower mosque, not only from the municipality of Vitez but beyond, and at that time, were there any pilgrimages to this new mosque, because if this would be a mosque of wider significance for other Muslims, then people would go there on pilgrimages. They go to Mecca, Medina, and to the other holy places of the Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims do have a custom of Mevlud. That means that every village has a certain established date, to the best of my knowledge, for the Mevlud. I think that Ahmici had a certain date for the upper mosque and that Hazim, with the assistance of his son Zaim who is a hodza and who lives in Vienna, managed to organise very often the Mevlud which was held at his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me one more thing. This is something I've heard for the very first time today, Mevlud. It's the first time I've heard this word. Could you please explain this to me and the Court? Is it some kind of a fair or what?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, Mevlud, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a prosession?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is a ceremonious prayer. It does not involve prayer only but also religious songs and chants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was done in connection with this Mevlud in the lower mosque? Did it differ from the Mevluds at other mosques?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it did not differ from them, but prominent religious leaders from other communities would come in, and I think that this was under the influence of his son Zaim, and I believe that he had quite a few acquaintances in these circles, because it was in the interests of his son Zaim for this mosque to stay on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was anything controversial as to whether it would remain or not?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if a mosque does not have believers who come there, then it would be controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Then the Prosecutor asked you about labour relations. Tell me about the period before the free elections and after the free elections and before the armed conflicts broke out. What were the regulations governing the area of labour? Notably, were there any special regulations pertaining to labour relations within PTT organisations, of course, if you know about this?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until the war, we, at the post office, all worked according to rules and regulations and laws that were prescribed by the then community of Yugoslav PTT, and all our regulations that were in force at the time actually date back to those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is that to say that after the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina gained its independence, previous rules and regulations from the former Yugoslavia were not infringed upon in any way?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they were not infringed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you continued to work as you did before that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this go on?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as the post office was concerned, this went on until 1994, November 1994, when a new form of PTT enterprises was introduced in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So it was only then that these rules and regulations on labour relations for the former Yugoslavia ceased to be applied?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, from these rules and regulations, what the term was for cessation of a labour relationship? That is, when would one lose his job after not coming to work for a certain number of days?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if a person would not come to work after a certain number of days, then his superior would report this and would initiate proceedings. This meant disciplinary action --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard enough about this. It's a small issue about what happened on the 20th of October, and we've heard, as far as I can see, all the evidence that's necessary. We don't need to go into a lot of evidence about labour relations, particularly historically. Could you move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not intend to put other questions related to this subject, but I did have to raise this particular question because the Prosecutor did not exhibit sufficient knowledge as to how the situation was regulated in the post office at that time, and that question was put by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So it turned out that in the Croat part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were some special rules and regulations, although that was not the case. Now, the Prosecutor also asked you about the current situation regarding the police, so please tell me, you explained that the chief of the police station at Vitez was a Muslim now; however, I'm interested in something else. A police patrol exists of two men, and when they go out to the field, what is their composition in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I think that the composition is half/half. I do not know the exact percentage, perhaps there's a bit more of one or the other, but it's roughly half/half, and this pertains to all services, even patrols. Patrols are mixed patrols. If there are two policemen on one patrol, then one is Muslim and the other one is a Croat or if there is four, then it is half/half, to the best of my knowledge when I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you followed the newspapers, and that is how you received information; did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, which newspapers did you read?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, the only newspapers that could be read was Oslobodjenje from Sarajevo and Vecernje List from Sarajevo. I think it was called Vecernje Novine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So there were no Croatian newspapers there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Also, the Prosecutor asked you about the intentions of Herceg-Bosna. Where were political decisions reached?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, at the highest party level of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about within Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think that such decisions were made within Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever see or hear of any political decision being made by the accused Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic or did you see any document which would be issuing anyone any kind of orders that was signed by them?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, never did I see or hear anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was their position such that they could reach a political decision that would be binding on anyone?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no, certainly not, certainly not. They were not in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The same question relates to their military powers. Did Mirjan or Zoran Kupreskic have any powers, any authority, to give any kind of order to any military unit?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any military orders issued by Mirjan or Zoran Kupreskic ordering anybody to do anything?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I never had the opportunity of seeing anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you about the alert and reporting system, and again I see that there has been a lack of understanding there; therefore, I shall have to re-examine on that score so that we would clarify this misunderstanding. Tell me, the reporting and alert centre, did it inform citizens about certain events as they were taking place or after they would take place?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think that it depends on the event concerned, but just one detail. When Vitez was shelled by the JNA, the reporting centre informed the citizens that there would be danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but on the basis of what information?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, when the shelling took place or when the aeroplanes arrived?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, when the aeroplanes arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When the aeroplanes arrived, there was bombing; right? I apologise. Yes, I'm talking about bombing. Other cases?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Other cases, well, when they are reported, when citizens report a fire or a flood, then information was given to the rest of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So in principle, when there was imminent danger, then they would report; right?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document with a list of persons killed. Ms. Slokovic-Glumac said that she will be dealing with that, so I shall omit that question. Tell me, you know where the Ogrjev warehouse was, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You described it already and you described the fence, et cetera. Could you tell me whether on your computer, on the 16th of April, 1993, there was any information that the telephone lines with Ogrjev had broken down?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to explain the kind of information that was provided by the computer in general. If the cable would break down without the lines actually touching one another, the computer did not register that on this list, unless the computer was given exactly that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you cannot answer that question of mine?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. If the telephone was not plugged into the wall, the computer would not be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I'm not asking you that. I'm not asking you whether the computer was not plugged into the wall. I'm asking you whether there was any information that the line towards Ogrjev was broken down, and, therefore, because this line was broken down, all other telephones were disconnected. Can you tell me about that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall whether that number was also on the list, but on the first day, there were some numbers from that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean that line?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that line. There were numbers that did not operate --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know whether all of them were inoperative --

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I also don't know and I cannot remember whether the Ogrjev number was out of order too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. The Prosecutor asked you about your sister's encounter with the village guards. It was put a bit differently, as compared to your own testimony, so let's see, who did your sister see? Did they say that she met the village guards, and she probably would have known all the village guards, or when she met these armed, uniformed men, were there some men she didn't know among them?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: She encountered a group, and there were quite a few neighbours in this group. All of them were armed. She can give all their names. The group was led by --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But were there any persons she did not know within that group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were some persons she did not know, but I don't know how many. That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have thus concluded my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, can we take another look at the list that is being mentioned. Tell me one thing: According to existing regulations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the former Yugoslavia, how did you determine the date of somebody's death? What document was an official document issued on the occasion of somebody's death?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the official valid document was the death certificate, with the doctor's certificate, the doctor that performs the final examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: According to the death certificate, does the death certificate state the time of death, the date of death, and the place of death? Does this basic data appear in the death certificate?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that it does, yes. And the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Are they reliable data?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, they should be, yes. I think -- yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So an official document?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: If the coroner has signed the document, then it does have the weight of an official document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The death certificate given out by the competent authorities in a municipality, that is to say when you reach -- gain information on a death in the municipality and the official writes out this document, is that a relevant, valid document?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And is that the type of certificate, the document that is issued in the municipality, is the presence of a physician required?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well, then. You have seen the list; you said you didn't know what it was. And if you had death certificates on the other side, which of these two documents would you say was a reliable document: The death certificate, or the document you were shown?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think the list with a supplement of the death certificates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: If you had different information in the death certificates that differed from this list, would you think that the death certificate was valid? Would that be the one you would believe and trust? Or the list? What would you opt for?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would believe the death certificates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, on page 1, take a look, and it says the list of members of the HVO who were killed; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you turn to page 10, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Defence counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Page 10 of the Croatian text, please. Take a look at that. Which of these individuals could have been members of the HVO, and who were people of the military-able age? How old were they? By law.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I think up to the age of 50, that that was considered military age, from the ages of 18 to 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the individuals numbered 512, 513, 514, 518, 519, 520.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can see those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: 523, 524, 525, 526, and take a look at their date of birth, which is found in the first column. And year, next to the names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all comment, really. Rather than going through the witness, you can make these points in argument, Miss Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't really need endless evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, Your Honour, but in view of the fact that the Prosecutor has been referring to this document on a number of occasions, and it is such an erroneous one, that it would be of assistance to me to have comments from the witness himself. But you are of course absolutely right, Your Honour, so we'll skip over that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, with regard to the other facts that appear here, whether the place of Ahmici is mentioned. You said that other places appear, such as Santici, Pirici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were they places which are very close to Ahmici? That is to say whether, according to the best of your knowledge, there were any combat operations on the 16th of April, 1993 there.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my testimony and what I explained was that the Ahmici municipality includes the Gornji Pirici, Nadioci, Gornji/Donji Ahmici villages, which means --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any conflict on the 16th there, to the best of your knowledge, in the area of Pirici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Santici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Referring to another part of your testimony, you were asked again about the 15th. Tell us, please, what you did on the 15th. You went to work, you came home at about -- when did you complete your shift?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th I completed my shift at 3.00 p.m. As on every other day, at 3.00 in the afternoon, that was when my work ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I started out for home, and I stopped off in a shop to buy some things, some food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went to the department store in Vitez, and a shop which was in the building of my own apartment, in the entrance to my building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What shop is that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: The shop was called PP Sutra, belonging to the Sutra enterprise, and it sold foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who did you see there? Who works there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mirjan Kupreskic worked there. He was a salesman. He worked there for a year after the shop had been opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were asked whether you had seen him -- you saw him for the last time on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, on that day, I bought -- I can't tell you the exact number, but I bought several tins of goulash, of beef stew there, and a Tuborg beer. That was the only shop where you were able to purchase Tuborg beer, and we both had a beer on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see him again on that day? Do you know how long he worked in the shop, in view of the fact that you lived in the building yourself?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think I was in the shop at 4.00 in the afternoon, and then went up to my apartment, and thought that I would be doing my shift that evening. I didn't see him again on that day except for that meeting in the shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What else did you do on that particular day, before your night shift? Did you have any other activities?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not in my apartment. We had a baby, the baby was five months old, and I spent that time with my baby, my little baby girl.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And when did your night shift begin? I forgot to ask you.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: At 8 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Up until that time was everything quiet in Vitez? Was it a normal working day for you?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was, a normal working day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see any increased movement when you came from your work or when you went to work in the evening, did you see any movement of the military of any kind, a large number of soldiers, or was it -- what was the situation like, generally speaking, in the evening when you went back to work?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: In town, I didn't see any movement of any kind, anything that would be out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One more question in connection with Ahmici: Can you remember, on the morning when you went through the list of numbers, what had happened to the telephone numbers in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember that. On that particular morning, my first request after the alarm list, the computer printed out a list of a possible 150 or more numbers, subscriber telephone numbers, which were down. In comparison to Ahmici, in that area, on that list there were numbers which were charged from one of our -- one of the cupboards, power cupboards, below my mother's house, and this supplied the electricity supplies for that entire region. So it was these power cabinets, and there was a short circuit there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you mean the telephone lines around your mother's house were down, or were they out of order in a broader area?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: This source, which was the source for my mother's lines and for the first houses in Ahmici, the aerial cable which went up to Gornji Ahmici passed across the house and through the house of Vlatko Kupreskic and then went upwards. So this whole area and this whole direction at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Srevne Ahmici, where the Kupreskic houses too, the telephone lines were out of order there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the middle level Ahmicis did not receive their power supply from that line. (redacted) (redacted) those were the exceptions Ahmic Hazim's house, and I think Mustafer's as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So all the others had -- their telephone lines were in operation in the morning?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vidovic, for testifying in Court. You may now be released. And we adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
